title: Blooming of the Spare Tyre Nebula
caption: The Spare Tyre Nebula, IC 5148, imaged by the Gemini South telescope
celestial: IC 5148 · constellation Grus · about 3000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Image processing: T.A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Rodriguez (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), & M. Zamani (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Asymmetrical blooms of gas and a faint halo ring surround a central star, with a dark hole around it, in this Gemini South image of IC 5148, the Spare Tyre Nebula. This planetary nebula lies about 3000 light-years away near the 'neck' of the southern constellation Grus, the Crane.

The star at its centre is a white dwarf, the hot core of a dying star that was likely similar in mass to the Sun. Late in life, that star swelled into a red giant, and its outer layers were pushed into space to form the nebula. The dark hole exists because radiation pressure from the star shoves nearby gas away from the core. How the ring and the bow-like structures formed is still a mystery.

IC 5148 is one of the fastest-expanding planetary nebulae, moving outward at 180,000 kilometres per hour. Small telescopes show only a bright star with a ring; its faint layers need larger instruments to be seen this clearly.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (5.51 x 4.93 arcminutes) and distance (3000 light years), the frame spans roughly 4.8 × 4.3 light-years. Its light set out about 3,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with GMOS on Gemini South through g, r, i, hydrogen-alpha and [O III] filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Through small telescopes the nebula looks like a bright star with a ring; the long exposure on a large telescope reveals faint layers the eye would miss.

explore: IC 5148 was discovered in 1894, around the time researchers coined the term planetary nebula for these gas clouds that resembled giant planets; today they are known to be stellar remnants. This view used the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS), and the expansion speed equals about 112,000 miles per hour.
alt: A planetary nebula with asymmetrical blooms of gas and a faint halo ring around a central star sitting in a dark hole.
